title: The boy who answered with a song
hookLine: milk on a small boy's lips, and a father who wants to know who gave it
carry: for the saints, singing to God is worship

lines: A BOY ON THE TEMPLE STEPS.
cards: A father leaves his little boy on the steps of a temple tank and wades in to bathe, ducking under the water to say his prayers.
On the steps, the boy can't see his father and starts to cry, calling for his mother and father, looking toward the temple tower. When the father comes up, the crying has stopped. The boy is calm.
And there's milk on his lips. Nobody else is there.

teach.b: The town is Sirkazhi, and the boy is known as Sambandar. In the Periya Puranam, when he cries, Shiva and Parvati come to the tank, and Parvati, the Mother of the world, feeds him milk from a golden cup. Then they're gone.
His father, a careful Brahmin, sees the milk and is furious.
Who fed you? Food from a stranger's hand could break the rules he lives by. He picks up a stick.
And the small boy, instead of explaining, points up at the sky and sings.
That song, as tradition remembers it, describes the one who wears an earring in his ear, who rides the bull, who wears the pale crescent moon, and then calls him the thief who stole my heart.
The boy's answer to who fed you is: him. And his answer comes as a song.

That's the heart of bhakti, loving devotion, as the Tamil saints lived it: you don't only think about God, you sing to him, and the singing itself is worship. Sambandar sang all his life, from temple to temple.
His songs, with those of Appar and Sundarar, are gathered as the Tevaram, and in Tamil Shiva temples, singers called oduvars still sing them in worship.
It's a big part of why so much Hindu devotion is sung: bhajans in living rooms, kirtan in temples. Kannappa offered with his hands, Karaikkal Ammaiyar at her door, Sambandar with his voice.

how: Tamil Shaivas sing hymns from the Tevaram in temple worship, often led by singers called oduvars, and the story of Sambandar and the milk is remembered at the Sirkazhi temple.

o: the singers who lead worship at the temple tank
the Brahmin fathers of the temple town Sirkazhi
Shiva's Tamil saints, Sambandar among them

games.q: Sambandar's first song — tap the pairs.
p: fed the boy milk from a golden cup
asks who fed you, stick in hand
singers who lead the Tevaram in worship

s: for the Tamil saints, singing was only a way to remember the stories
the singing itself was worship, and the Tevaram is still sung in temple worship.
the song calls Shiva the thief who stole my heart
after describing the earring, the bull and the crescent moon.
the story makes the father a villain
he's a man of rules, afraid for his son, and the story answers him with a song.

games.q: you're the small boy. your father is standing over you with a stick, asking who gave you milk. what do you do?
o: point at the sky and sing.
blame a stranger who walked by.
games.why: he points up and sings his first hymn. his answer is Shiva, and his way of saying it is a song: in bhakti, singing to God is worship.

practice: Choose a name of God you know, Shiva, Krishna, Ram, or simply Om, and sing it softly on one easy note, three times, the way many bhajans begin. It doesn't have to be good; a child's voice was enough.
If you pray, let the singing be the prayer. If you don't, hum one note and listen to it, and think of someone who fed you when you thought you were alone.

wordCard.voice: The Nayanars. The Tamil saints of Shiva. Sambandar is the boy fed milk by Parvati, whose songs are sung in the Tevaram.

orig.note: Tamil: the name for the gathered hymns of Sambandar, Appar and Sundarar.
